samples.title: Energy optimization in smart urban buildings using bio-inspired ant colony optimization

anchor_claims.text: A hybrid optimization algorithm, combining Bacterial Foraging Algorithm (BFA) and Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), called HB-ACO, is proposed for Home Energy Management Systems (HEMS) to optimize the scheduling of home appliances, reduce electricity costs, minimize peak-to-average ratio (PAR), and improve user comfort through day-ahead and real-time scheduling.

The HB-ACO algorithm replaces the elimination and dispersal step of BFA with ACO's pheromone update and probability selection mechanism to improve search efficiency and achieve better performance in load scheduling.

The proposed HB-ACO algorithm demonstrates superior performance compared to standalone BFA and ACO in reducing electricity costs and PAR while maintaining lower waiting times for appliances under both Time of Use (ToU) and Critical Peak Pricing (CPP) schemes.

Real-time scheduling in the proposed Home Energy Management System is modeled as a binary knapsack problem, where the remaining time of interrupted appliances is reallocated to high-priority appliances using the Ant Colony Optimization algorithm to reduce waiting times and enhance user comfort.

The proposed HB-ACO algorithm achieves a tradeoff between electricity cost, peak-to-average ratio, and user comfort, addressing the limitations of existing methods that often fail to optimize all three parameters simultaneously.

### Summary

Smart urban buildings face the complex challenge of balancing energy efficiency, cost reduction, and user comfort amid increasing demand for sustainable and intelligent building management systems. To address these needs, **bio-inspired ant colony optimization (ACO) algorithms**, particularly hybrid variants integrating ACO with other bio-inspired optimizers such as bacterial foraging, particle swarm optimization (PSO), and other nature-inspired techniques, have emerged as powerful tools for optimizing energy performance.

These algorithms mimic the collective behavior of biological organisms like ants and swarm animals to efficiently solve multi-objective optimization problems relevant to building energy systems. Key applications include **smart home appliance scheduling**, **energy dispatch in microgrids and grid-connected systems**, and **wireless sensor network (WSN) management** in urban environments.

Hybrid approaches such as the **HB-ACO algorithm** combine the pheromone-based pathfinding of ACO with elements from bacterial foraging (elimination/dispersal replacement) to accelerate search, improving convergence and solution quality for problems like **time-of-use (ToU) and critical peak pricing (CPP) energy scheduling**. These methods not only reduce electricity costs and minimize the **peak-to-average ratio (PAR)** but also maintain user comfort through dynamic load scheduling and real-time adaptation.

The bio-inspired ACO and its hybrids are effectively employed for **building-level optimization** (e.g., triple-layer glass thickness for solar heat management) as well as city-scale applications, including **smart city energy management** that orchestrates distributed energy resources (DERs) and IoT-enabled devices. By leveraging cross-layer design and governance frameworks incorporating ACO, these systems optimize **clustering, routing, and resource allocation in sensor networks**, further extending energy efficiency gains across urban infrastructures.

Simulation and experimental results consistently demonstrate that these bio-inspired ACO-based algorithms outperform traditional metaheuristics and standalone algorithms in reducing operational costs, energy losses, and increasing network/lifetime longevity. They also show robustness in handling high-dimensional, dynamic, and multi-objective challenges, such as balancing renewable energy utilization, grid integration, and emergency load management.

Moreover, extensions with machine learning (e.g., LSTM, random forest) and multi-objective optimization allow these algorithms to adapt to real-world complexities like changing weather, user behavior, and system faults. Future enhancements may include integration with real-time data, adaptive parameter tuning, and support for non-uniform and fault-prone environments.

In summary, **bio-inspired ant colony optimization and its hybrids represent a leading paradigm for energy optimization in smart urban buildings**, providing efficient, scalable, and adaptive solutions to meet the dual objectives of sustainable energy management and improved occupant comfort within complex, dynamic urban infrastructures.

**Summary: Energy Optimization in Smart Urban Buildings Using Ant Colony Optimization and Bio-Inspired Algorithms**

Recent advances in energy management for smart urban buildings increasingly leverage bio-inspired optimization algorithms, with Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) being a central and well-studied approach. These bio-inspired methods mimic natural behaviors—such as those observed in ants, birds, and marine organisms—to solve complex energy optimization problems efficiently.

One prominent hybrid solution is the **Hybrid Ant Colony Optimization (HB-ACO)** algorithm. HB-ACO combines elements of ACO with the Foraging Behavior of the Bacterial Foraging Algorithm (BFA), specifically replacing the dispersal and elimination phases of BFA with ACO’s pheromone updating and probability selection. This fusion enhances search efficiency and enables the optimization of critical energy scheduling parameters in smart homes and urban environments. It is particularly applied to the complex problem of **appliance and load scheduling**, aiming to minimize electricity costs, reduce the peak-to-average power ratio (PAR), and maintain user comfort across both **day-ahead and real-time** energy management scenarios.

In practical smart building applications, HB-ACO is often integrated within **Home Energy Management Systems (HEMS)** where the optimization targets the real-time allocation and rescheduling of appliances, modeling tasks as combinatorial optimization problems—such as the binary knapsack problem. This ensures not only cost and energy savings but also faster response to dynamic demand and emergency load interruptions by intelligently rebalancing loads among high-priority devices.

Extensive research shows that HB-ACO, and broadly ACO and related bio-inspired algorithms, outperform traditional or single metaheuristic approaches in reducing energy costs and the peak demand while simultaneously improving system responsiveness and user comfort. When extended to smart city contexts or large-scale energy management, related bio-inspired algorithms—such as Quantum Firefly Swarm Optimization (QF-PSO), Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), and others—combine governance and adaptive intelligence to optimize sensor networks, load distribution, and overall energy efficiency in urban infrastructures.

In summary, **bio-inspired algorithms, with ACO as a core technique, provide powerful, scalable, and efficient means to optimize energy usage in smart urban buildings**, enabling more cost-effective, sustainable, and responsive energy control systems that integrate seamlessly with modern IoT and smart grid infrastructures.

Summary: Energy Optimization in Smart Urban Buildings Using Ant Colony Optimization and Bio-Inspired Algorithms

Energy optimization in smart urban buildings is increasingly formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem involving energy consumption, electricity cost, peak demand, renewable-energy utilization, occupant requirements, and the reliability of associated communication and sensing infrastructure. Bio-inspired optimization algorithms provide a useful framework for these problems because they can search large, nonlinear, and discrete solution spaces without requiring an exact analytical model of the entire energy system.

Among these approaches, Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) is particularly relevant to discrete decision problems such as appliance scheduling, routing, resource allocation, and configuration selection. ACO uses the collective search behavior of artificial ants, where promising solutions receive stronger pheromone reinforcement and consequently become more likely to be explored in subsequent iterations. This combination of probabilistic exploration and iterative reinforcement allows ACO to progressively identify high-quality solutions while retaining some ability to explore alternatives. Beyond buildings themselves, ACO has been applied extensively to energy-aware routing and resource allocation in wireless sensor, ad hoc, IoT, and other distributed systems, demonstrating the general applicability of pheromone-driven optimization to resource-constrained environments.

The literature also indicates that hybrid bio-inspired optimization can be advantageous when a single metaheuristic has limitations in exploration, exploitation, convergence, or computational efficiency. ACO has therefore been combined or compared with approaches such as Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Genetic Algorithms (GA), Artificial Bee Colony (ABC), Grey Wolf Optimization, and other swarm and evolutionary methods. Such combinations aim to exploit complementary search properties, for example using one mechanism for broad exploration of the solution space and another for refinement around promising solutions. Similar hybrid approaches have been investigated for distributed energy-resource scheduling, microgrids, building energy management, renewable-energy systems, and energy-efficient IoT networks.

In smart building energy management, optimization increasingly operates within an IoT-enabled architecture incorporating smart meters, sensors, distributed energy resources, energy storage, electric vehicles, and controllable loads. These components provide real-time information that enables an energy-management system to coordinate electricity consumption rather than treating individual devices independently. Bio-inspired optimization can consequently be applied to scheduling flexible loads, reducing demand peaks, coordinating local generation and storage, and responding to dynamic electricity prices. This makes the optimization problem inherently multi-objective, since minimizing electricity expenditure alone can produce undesirable demand peaks or reduce occupant convenience.

A related body of work highlights the importance of the communication and sensing infrastructure supporting building energy management. ACO and other bio-inspired methods have been used for energy-aware routing, cluster-head selection, load balancing, and resource allocation in wireless sensor and IoT networks. Optimizing these supporting systems can reduce communication energy consumption and extend network lifetime, which is particularly relevant for large-scale smart buildings containing many distributed sensing and control devices.

More broadly, emerging approaches combine metaheuristics with machine learning, reinforcement learning, federated learning, predictive analytics, and edge computing. This creates an important distinction between conventional bio-inspired optimization and adaptive intelligent energy management. A metaheuristic such as ACO can efficiently search a combinatorial decision space, while learning-based models can predict future demand, renewable generation, environmental conditions, or system states. Edge computing can further move some optimization decisions closer to individual buildings or devices, reducing communication requirements and enabling faster local responses.

Overall, the literature suggests that the value of ACO in smart urban energy systems lies not in a single specific algorithmic configuration, but in its broader ability to support decentralized, adaptive, and multi-objective optimization. The strongest research direction appears to be toward hybrid systems in which ACO or related swarm intelligence methods operate alongside predictive AI, distributed sensing, renewable generation, storage, and real-time control. However, performance claims remain highly dependent on problem formulation, parameter settings, datasets, simulation assumptions, and comparison baselines. Consequently, no individual bio-inspired algorithm can be considered universally superior; algorithms should instead be evaluated under consistent and realistic building-energy scenarios.

Retraction note: The supplied context states that Energy optimization in smart urban buildings using bio-inspired ant colony optimization has been retracted. Therefore, specific claims associated with that paper, including its HB-ACO method, its reported superiority over standalone BFA/ACO, and its quantitative or qualitative scheduling benefits, have not been treated as supporting evidence in this synthesis. This is important because otherwise the repeated claims from that paper could disproportionately influence the apparent consensus of the literature.

Their flexibility makes them particularly applicable to nonlinear, combinatorial, and multi-objective optimization problems encountered in building energy management, distributed energy resources, and smart grids.

Ant Colony Optimization is especially relevant to discrete optimization problems such as appliance scheduling, resource allocation, network routing, and configuration selection. Inspired by the pheromone-based collective behavior of ants, ACO constructs candidate solutions probabilistically and reinforces successful choices through iterative pheromone updates. The supplied literature demonstrates the broader utility of this mechanism in energy-aware wireless sensor networks, consumer home-automation networks, smart grids, and distributed systems. ACO-based methods can incorporate factors such as residual energy, communication cost, route length, load conditions, and service requirements into their decisions. This makes ACO useful not only for optimizing electricity-related decisions but also for improving the efficiency of the IoT and communication infrastructure supporting smart buildings.

At the building and microgrid level, bio-inspired algorithms are used to coordinate controllable loads, renewable energy sources, energy-storage systems, electric vehicles, and grid interactions. This allows energy-management systems to respond dynamically to changing demand, electricity prices, and renewable generation. The literature indicates that such optimization can target multiple objectives simultaneously, including reduced operating costs and peak-to-average ratio, increased renewable-energy utilization, and preservation of occupant comfort. IoT-enabled sensing and smart meters further provide the real-time information needed for adaptive building energy management rather than relying solely on fixed scheduling rules.

An important trend is the development of hybrid bio-inspired algorithms. Instead of assuming that one metaheuristic is universally optimal, researchers combine mechanisms from PSO, GA, ACO, ABC, Grey Wolf Optimization, Whale Optimization, and other approaches. These combinations seek to compensate for limitations such as premature convergence, slow search, parameter sensitivity, or inadequate exploration. The supplied studies on wireless sensor networks, distributed energy scheduling, and other optimization domains suggest that hybrid approaches can benefit from combining the global-search capabilities of one algorithm with the local refinement capabilities of another. However, performance is problem-dependent, and comparisons between algorithms should therefore consider identical objective functions, constraints, computational budgets, datasets, and experimental conditions.

A second important development is the integration of bio-inspired optimization with AI, IoT, edge computing, and distributed intelligence. Smart-building energy systems increasingly generate real-time information from HVAC systems, lighting, smart appliances, EV charging, energy storage, renewable generation, and environmental sensors. Predictive models can estimate future demand or renewable availability, while optimization algorithms determine appropriate control actions. Edge and decentralized architectures can move these decisions closer to buildings and devices, potentially reducing communication latency and network overhead. The supplied literature also points toward integration with reinforcement learning, federated learning, predictive analytics, and multi-agent approaches as a direction for increasingly adaptive energy-management systems.

Energy optimization also extends to the supporting infrastructure of smart urban buildings. ACO and other bio-inspired approaches have been applied to energy-efficient routing, sensor clustering, packet scheduling, load balancing, and wireless access-point placement. Reducing the communication energy consumed by large networks of sensors can contribute to overall system efficiency and extend the operating lifetime of battery-powered IoT devices. Consequently, smart-building energy optimization can be viewed as a multi-layer problem encompassing physical energy consumption, DER coordination, sensing, communication, computation, and control.

Overall, the supplied literature supports a broader research direction in which bio-inspired optimization provides flexible search mechanisms for complex smart-building and urban-energy problems, while ACO provides a particularly natural mechanism for discrete, distributed, and path-dependent decisions. Hybridization with other metaheuristics and integration with predictive AI and edge computing may make these methods more responsive to dynamic environments. Nevertheless, practical adoption continues to face challenges including computational complexity, parameter tuning, scalability, interoperability, cybersecurity, uncertainty, and the gap between simulation-based evaluation and deployment in operating buildings.

**Fusion of Multi-Modality Biomedical Images using Deep Neural Networks in Radiology Imaging**

Fusion of multi-modality biomedical images has emerged as a crucial aspect of radiology imaging, enabling the combination of complementary information from different imaging modalities to enhance diagnostic accuracy and decision-making. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been successfully employed to fuse multi-modality biomedical images, leveraging their ability to learn complex patterns and relationships between modalities.

**Key Approaches:**

1. **Layer-wise Fusion**: This approach involves combining features from different modalities at various layers of a DNN, allowing for the fusion of complementary information at different levels of abstraction.
2. **Modality-aware Features**: This approach involves learning features that are specific to each modality, enabling the DNN to capture modality-specific information and fuse it with information from other modalities.
3. **Inter-modality Similarities**: This approach involves learning similarities between modalities, enabling the DNN to fuse information from different modalities based on their relationships.

**Methods and Techniques:**

1. **Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)**: CNNs have been widely used for multi-modality image fusion, leveraging their ability to learn spatial hierarchies and feature representations.
2. **Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)**: GANs have been employed for multi-modality image fusion, enabling the generation of high-quality fused images that preserve the characteristics of individual modalities.
3. **Ensemble Learning**: Ensemble learning approaches have been used to combine the predictions of multiple models, improving the accuracy and robustness of multi-modality image fusion.
4. **Attention Mechanisms**: Attention mechanisms have been employed to selectively focus on relevant regions of interest, improving the performance of multi-modality image fusion.

**Applications and Evaluations:**

1. **Alzheimer's Disease Detection**: Multi-modality image fusion has been successfully employed for Alzheimer's disease detection, improving the accuracy and robustness of diagnosis.
2. **Brain Tumor Segmentation**: Multi-modality image fusion has been used for brain tumor segmentation, enabling the accurate detection and delineation of tumors.
3. **Breast Cancer Detection**: Multi-modality image fusion has been employed for breast cancer detection, improving the accuracy and sensitivity of diagnosis.
4. **Cardiovascular Disease Detection**: Multi-modality image fusion has been used for cardiovascular disease detection, enabling the accurate diagnosis and prediction of disease progression.

**Challenges and Future Directions:**

1. **Data Quality and Availability**: The availability and quality of multi-modality image data pose significant challenges to the development and evaluation of fusion techniques.
2. **Interoperability and Standardization**: The lack of interoperability and standardization between different imaging modalities and systems hinders the development and adoption of fusion techniques.

4. **Clinical Adoption and Integration**: The successful adoption and integration of fusion techniques into clinical practice require addressing challenges related to workflow, user interface, and clinical acceptance.

Below is a consolidated summary based only on the supplied titles and claims, emphasizing deep neural network approaches for multimodality biomedical and radiological image fusion.

Summary

Fusion of multimodality biomedical images using deep neural networks is an increasingly important approach in radiology for integrating complementary information from imaging modalities such as MRI, CT, PET, SPECT, and ultrasound. Different modalities capture distinct anatomical, structural, functional, or metabolic characteristics. Deep learning-based fusion seeks to combine these characteristics into unified image or feature representations that preserve diagnostically significant information and potentially improve visualization, segmentation, classification, and clinical decision support.

A central direction is modality-aware representation learning. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and related architectures extract modality-specific and shared features before combining them using pixel-level, feature-level, or decision-level fusion. Layer-wise and attention-based strategies can selectively preserve useful information from individual modalities while exploiting inter-modality similarities. Alternative approaches decompose images into structural and detail components, fuse them separately, and reconstruct the final image. Other frameworks incorporate non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), weighted feature averaging, gradient-based adaptive weighting, and disentangled representations to retain natural structures and modality-specific diagnostic details.

More sophisticated approaches extend conventional CNN fusion with transformers, graph neural networks, contrastive learning, autoencoders, GANs, and VAEs. Transformer-based attention can model long-range spatial relationships, while graph-aware mechanisms explicitly capture relationships among regions and modalities. Contrastive fusion encourages semantic alignment between modalities while maintaining complementary information. Generative approaches such as GANs and VAEs can produce spatially coherent fused representations, support feature disentanglement, and potentially model uncertainty. Attention mechanisms are particularly useful for assigning greater importance to diagnostically relevant regions rather than treating every modality or feature equally.

Optimization of the fusion process is another recurring theme. Multi-objective differential evolution, particle swarm optimization, genetic algorithms, and other nature-inspired methods have been used for feature selection or optimization of network hyperparameters and fusion parameters. Such approaches seek a balance among competing image-quality objectives, including information preservation and edge strength. Adaptive quality-driven fusion can additionally use local gradient, visibility, exposure, and consistency information to determine pixel-wise or feature-wise contribution from each modality.

Evidence summarized in the supplied literature indicates that deep learning fusion frequently performs better than traditional methods such as PCA, discrete wavelet transforms, and related transform-based fusion techniques. Reported assessments use measures including entropy, mutual information, standard deviation, fusion factor, fusion symmetry, average gradient, edge intensity, spatial frequency, SSIM, PSNR, Dice score, IoU, and downstream classification accuracy. Several studies also report improvements over unimodal approaches, suggesting that combining complementary modalities can benefit applications including brain tumor analysis, Alzheimer's disease detection, pancreatic lesion diagnosis, breast tumor classification, heart disease assessment, and multi-atlas segmentation.

For radiology specifically, multimodality fusion can bring together complementary characteristics such as the soft-tissue information of MRI, structural information from CT, metabolic or functional information from PET/SPECT, and complementary characteristics provided by ultrasound. Importantly, fusion is not limited to creating a new composite image. Deep neural networks can also fuse intermediate representations for downstream segmentation or diagnosis, allowing relevant information from each modality to contribute directly to the clinical prediction.

Despite promising results, important challenges remain. These include limited model interpretability, high computational and training-data requirements, loss of modality-specific information, sensitivity to image registration, heterogeneity among imaging protocols, insufficient cross-dataset generalization, and limited clinical validation. Explainability approaches such as Grad-CAM and SHAP, uncertainty estimation, domain adaptation, and disentangled modality representations are therefore becoming important components of clinically oriented fusion systems.

Overall, the literature suggests a shift from fixed, hand-engineered fusion rules toward adaptive and context-aware deep neural fusion. Future radiological systems are likely to emphasize lightweight architectures, attention and transformer mechanisms, explainable AI, uncertainty-aware predictions, robust cross-domain generalization, standardized benchmarks, and prospective clinical validation. The key objective is not simply to produce visually appealing fused images, but to create reliable and interpretable multimodal representations that preserve clinically meaningful information and measurably improve radiological diagnosis and decision-making.

Multi-modality biomedical image fusion aims to combine complementary information from radiological imaging modalities such as MRI, CT, PET, SPECT, and ultrasound into unified representations that preserve diagnostically important anatomical and functional information. Deep neural networks, particularly CNN-based architectures, attention mechanisms, autoencoders, transformers, and generative models, can learn modality-specific and shared representations and perform fusion at pixel, feature, or decision levels. Compared with conventional approaches such as PCA, wavelet transforms, and other transform-based techniques, deep-learning fusion is intended to improve feature extraction, structural-detail preservation, and the integration of complementary imaging information.

The supplied literature suggests several recurring technical directions. These include modality-aware feature extraction, layer-wise or attention-based feature fusion, decomposition of images into structural and detail components, and separation of modality-specific features from representations shared across modalities. Other approaches combine deep networks with techniques such as non-negative matrix factorization, optimization algorithms, contrastive learning, graph neural networks, or generative models. Such architectures are being investigated both for producing a directly fused radiological image and for downstream applications including tumor segmentation, Alzheimer's disease classification, pancreatic lesion diagnosis, and other computer-aided diagnostic tasks.

A consistent theme is that successful fusion requires more than combining images. The model must preserve clinically meaningful details from each source modality while managing differences in spatial resolution, contrast, acquisition characteristics, noise, and alignment. Consequently, evaluation commonly considers measures of information preservation, structural and edge retention, image quality, and downstream diagnostic or segmentation performance. Emerging approaches also emphasize interpretability, uncertainty estimation, cross-domain generalization, computational efficiency, and robustness across scanners, datasets, and imaging protocols.

However, evidence of improved numerical image-quality metrics should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of improved clinical outcomes. Important barriers to radiology deployment include limited interpretability, heterogeneous or relatively small datasets, registration errors, high computational requirements, inadequate external validation, and uncertainty about generalization to different institutions and acquisition protocols. Clinically useful systems therefore require standardized benchmarking, independent validation, explainable predictions, and evaluation of whether fusion actually improves radiologist performance or patient-relevant decisions.

Importantly, the supplied metadata identifies “Fusion of multi-modality biomedical images using deep neural networks” as a retracted paper. Its specific reported architecture, differential-evolution optimization procedure, benchmark comparisons, and claims of superiority over nine competing methods should therefore not be treated as reliable scientific evidence or used to substantiate conclusions. The duplicated claims associated with that paper should likewise be excluded from an evidence synthesis. #### 1. **Automated and Enhanced HR Processes**
AI-powered HRM systems automate routine and repetitive tasks such as recruitment, resume screening, payroll processing, performance evaluation, and employee onboarding. By utilizing techniques like backpropagation neural networks, convolutional autoencoders, and transformer-based architectures, these systems process vast datasets with speed and reduced human error. For example, intelligent recruitment models analyze candidate information, skills, and experience to predict fit and streamline hiring timelines.

Interactive performance design emphasizes personalized user experiences by leveraging AI to tailor recommendations in real time. AI systems provide:
- **Personalized learning and development plans**, identifying skill gaps via analytics and recommending tailored training modules.

The provided literature presents artificial intelligence as a key enabler for designing interactive and intelligent Human Resource Management Systems (HRMS). Across the studies, AI shifts HR systems from primarily administrative platforms toward data-driven decision-support environments that support recruitment, compensation, training, performance management, employee engagement, retention, and strategic workforce planning.

A prominent design example is the AI-based salary forecasting system, which converts information extracted from applicants' resumes, including personal, educational, work-experience, social, job, and enterprise-related characteristics, into structured numerical features. A Back Propagation Neural Network (BPNN) with a 14:15:1 architecture is then used to predict salary levels. Optimization with the Nadam algorithm improves convergence and training efficiency compared with methods such as SGD, Adam, and RMSprop, while the reported BPNN approach also demonstrates stronger predictive performance than several conventional regression and neural-network alternatives. The results particularly identify job type, work experience, and education level as important salary determinants. This illustrates how AI can be embedded directly into HRMS design to provide predictive and personalized decision support.

More broadly, interactive AI-enabled HRMS can improve the employee and HR-manager experience through intelligent recruitment and resume screening, personalized learning recommendations, real-time performance feedback, predictive workforce analytics, sentiment analysis, virtual assistants, intelligent Q&A, and automated administrative processes. Such capabilities allow systems to respond dynamically to employee characteristics and organizational requirements rather than providing standardized HR services. Personalization is especially important in training and development, where AI can identify competency gaps and adapt learning content, recommendations, and development paths to individual needs.

The literature also associates AI-enabled HR systems with improvements in operational efficiency, decision-making speed and accuracy, employee performance, engagement, retention, and organizational productivity. Automation reduces repetitive HR workloads, while predictive analytics can support workforce planning, candidate selection, attrition forecasting, compensation, and performance interventions. Importantly, several studies indicate that these benefits depend not merely on deploying sophisticated algorithms but on integrating AI effectively with existing HR processes, organizational strategy, and employees' technological capabilities.

At the same time, the evidence emphasizes that interactive performance is both a technical and a human-centered design issue. Effective systems require reliable data, usable interfaces, transparent recommendations, appropriate feedback mechanisms, interoperability with organizational platforms, and continuous model monitoring. Employee acceptance is particularly significant because perceived usefulness, ease of use, trust, and digital competence can determine whether technically effective AI applications actually improve workplace outcomes.

AI-based HRMS also introduces substantial risks, including algorithmic bias, privacy and cybersecurity concerns, lack of explainability, employee resistance, job-displacement anxiety, excessive dependence on automated recommendations, and uncertainty about accountability. Claims that AI automatically eliminates human bias should therefore be treated cautiously. AI may reduce some forms of subjective decision-making, but biased training data, model assumptions, or deployment practices can reproduce or amplify inequalities.

Consequently, the literature converges on a hybrid human-AI model as the most appropriate design direction. AI should automate routine activities, analyze complex data, generate predictions, and recommend possible actions, while human professionals retain oversight and responsibility for consequential HR decisions. Responsible system design should incorporate data governance, fairness assessment, algorithmic transparency and explainability, privacy protection, human review, employee participation, continuous auditing, and workforce reskilling.

Overall synthesis

An effective AI-based interactive Human Resource Management System can therefore be conceptualized around four interconnected layers:

Data layer: integrates resumes, employee records, qualifications, experience, performance information, skills, and organizational data.
AI and analytics layer: applies machine learning, neural networks, predictive analytics, recommendation systems, and related techniques for salary prediction, recruitment, attrition forecasting, training, and performance analysis.
Interactive HR layer: provides personalized recommendations, real-time feedback, dashboards, intelligent assistance, adaptive learning, and decision-support capabilities for employees and HR professionals.
Responsible governance layer: ensures privacy, security, fairness, explainability, accountability, human oversight, and continuous performance monitoring.

Overall, the research suggests that the strongest HRMS design is not an autonomous AI replacement for HR professionals, but an interactive, human-centered decision-support ecosystem. Its performance should therefore be evaluated not only through model accuracy and computational efficiency, but also through usability, employee acceptance, fairness, transparency, organizational outcomes, and long-term trust. Combining technically effective AI models with interactive design, ethical governance, and meaningful human oversight provides the most promising foundation for sustainable AI-enabled human resource management.

Summary of improvements

This synthesis consolidates the repeated claims into major themes rather than treating each study separately. It connects the specific BPNN/Nadam salary-prediction design with the broader literature on interactive HRMS, while distinguishing technical performance, human interaction, organizational benefits, and ethical governance as complementary dimensions of system design.

**Face Detection and Alignment:**  
Preprocessing steps such as face detection (often using cascaded classifiers or neural networks) and alignment normalize the input image to position the face centrally and standardize head pose. **Transfer-Learned Convolutional Feature Extraction:**  
A transfer-learned convolutional neural network (CNN), often based on a pre-trained model (e.g., AlexNet), leverages learned spatial and appearance features from large datasets and transfer knowledge to perform robust feature extraction even when the target dataset is limited or has differing conditions (e.g., varied lighting or expressions). Transfer learning reduces training time and data requirements while increasing model performance on face recognition tasks under challenging visual conditions. The network is typically fine-tuned on face images to adapt to the specific domain, improving accuracy compared to training from scratch.

**Fog–Cloud Deployment:**  
Fog–cloud computing architectures offload computationally intensive detection and feature extraction tasks to edge devices or network nodes ("fog"), while the more general or less variable recognition steps are processed in the cloud. This distributed approach reduces network latency and bandwidth usage by performing initial preprocessing and feature extraction locally (real-time, low-latency), then sending only compact feature vectors or identities to the cloud for final recognition and matching. This reduces load and speeds up the overall pipeline, particularly in environments with unreliable or limited connectivity (fog) or where privacy and data sensitivity are concerns (cloud). Additionally, it allows efficient handling of large numbers of concurrent face detections and minimizes delays caused by occlusions and challenging conditions at the local level.

Overall, this integrated pipeline improves recognition accuracy by robustly handling pose, illumination, expression, and occlusion through adaptive feature extraction and normalization, and increases processing efficiency by using resource-efficient transfer learning and distributed fog–cloud computation to reduce delays and computational overhead.

samples.title: Structure optimization and preparation of power system grounding grid based on similarity data analysis algorithm

anchor_claims.text: Flexible graphite composite grounding material, a non-metallic conductor made of graphite and synthetic fiber, offers advantages over traditional metal grounding materials such as reduced corrosion rate, lower inductance effect, and improved construction feasibility.

Grounding simulation tests based on similarity theory enable the study of actual grounding characteristics by constructing scaled-down models and extrapolating prototype parameters using dimensional analysis.

Distortion similarity terms, such as grounding electrode diameter and resistivity, can introduce significant errors in grounding simulation tests, limiting the application of similarity theory in grounding industry.

A distortion similarity model is defined to account for dependent variable π terms that do not satisfy complete similarity conditions, providing a mathematical framework for analyzing prediction errors in grounding simulation tests.
The distortion similarity model can be applied to simulation tests of various grounding materials and other power system scaling tests where complete similarity conditions cannot be met.

### 1. **Corrosion Rate**
- **Advantage:** Flexible graphite composite grounding materials are non-metallic and do not suffer from corrosion.
    - **Claim evidence:** (Reflected in the recurring themes of claims for non-metallic conductors made of graphite and synthetic fiber, compared to traditional metal grounding conductors)

---

### 2. **Inductance Effect**
- **Advantage:** Flexible graphite composites have lower inductance compared to metallic grounding rods.
    - **Claim evidence:**
        - *"improved construction feasibility" includes "reduced inductance effect"* (as summarized in the claim descriptions)
        - Metal grounding systems (such as grounding rods) can have higher self-inductance, leading to greater electromagnetic interference, slower transient response, and less effective fault current path dissipation.
        - Flexible graphite, with its conductive graphitic matrix embedded in a non-magnetic or low-inductance composite, offers a more direct and less inductive path for fault currents, improving system responsiveness and reliability during switching, surge, or fault events.
    - Lower inductance leads to better performance during high-frequency transients or lightning strikes.

---

### 3. **Construction Feasibility**
- **Advantage:** Flexible graphite composite materials are easier and safer to deploy in various site conditions, especially in difficult-to-access or environmentally sensitive locations.

### Advantages of Flexible Graphite Composite Grounding Material Compared to Traditional Metal Grounding Materials (as stated in the claim)

#### 1. **Reduced Corrosion Rate**
- **Flexible graphite composite** is a non-metal conductor (made from graphite with synthetic fibers).

- **Graphite** has inherently low chemical reactivity, lower susceptibility to corrosion than metals, hence **lower long-term maintenance and replacement costs**.

#### 2. **Lower Inductance Effect**
- Metal grounding rods and bars tend to have high self-induced inductance, especially in long or large-diameter conductors.
- **Graphite-based composites**, often in flexible forms, can be shaped to minimize inductive loop area and impedance, resulting in **reduced inductance losses** during transient faults.
- This means less inductive voltage drop under fault conditions, leading to potentially faster discharge of fault currents and improved system stability.

#### 3. **Improved Construction Feasibility**
- Traditional grounding systems often require large metal rod lengths or multiple rods, posing **difficulties in installation** in constrained or sensitive environments (e.g., coastal, saline, or rocky soils).
- **Graphite composite** can be molded into various shapes and sizes, has lighter weight (making handling easier), and can be installed in difficult terrains with less disturbance to the surrounding soil.
- **Synthetic fiber reinforcement** enhances mechanical strength and mechanical/electrical bonding, improving physical durability and handling.

The discrete elevation calculation algorithm improves the high-order stability of 3D landscape images by avoiding low visual rendering during the image generation process and optimizing edge correlation seed point matching.

Edge computing algorithms enhance the performance of landscape architecture design platforms by enabling local data processing, reducing image shaking, and improving the clarity and stability of 3D images.

The proposed landscape architecture 3D digital platform demonstrates superior performance in terms of user utility, uninstallation failure rates, and image stability compared to state-of-the-art algorithms such as random uninstallation, edge uninstallation, and uniform ratio algorithms.

The designed landscape architecture 3D digital platform provides a stable and high-definition display of 3D garden landscape images, achieving an average accuracy of over 90% and a Kappa coefficient of 86.93%, while maintaining a low frame loss rate and packet loss rate.

**Customer Features**  
E-commerce platforms capture a range of customer features—behaviors such as purchase frequency, recency, monetary value, browsing and click patterns, device usage, time since last purchase, and demographic information. These features, often encoded as structured or categorical data and normalized, provide the input signals for ML models. Latent or complex behaviors detected through clustering (e.g., RFM-based or K-Means/HAC methods) further refine segment identification by grouping customers with similar purchasing patterns.

**Model Design**  
Effective model design in e-commerce often involves selecting architectures that balance accuracy, interpretability, and scalability. Hybrid models (combining logistic regression with XGBoost, or using neural networks with ensemble methods) tend to outperform single models by mitigating overfitting and capturing both linear and nonlinear relationships in the data. Feature selection methods (e.g., SSP algorithm) can reduce model complexity, improving accuracy, especially with high-dimensional, sparse feature sets typical in e-commerce. Time-aware models and seasonality-aware architectures also capture patterns like holiday spikes in purchasing. Model evaluation uses classification metrics (accuracy, F1-score, AUC) and techniques such as cross-validation and handling class imbalance for robust predictions.

**Role of Data Sparsity**  
Customer behavior data in e-commerce can be highly sparse—many users purchase infrequently, creating uneven distribution of events (e.g., many low-frequency users and few frequent ones). This sparsity can limit the predictive performance of models, particularly those relying on precise probabilities for rare events. Some models mitigate this using oversampling, SMOTE (synthetic minority oversampling), or streaming/data-pipeline approaches that incrementally update models without needing full data retraining. In some cases, finer segmentation (e.g., one-to-one marketing for high-frequency users) benefits more than coarser segmentation from low-frequency users. Additionally, fusion algorithms or ensemble methods can help improve performance across sparse data scenarios by leveraging complementary hypotheses from multiple base models.

Combining segmentation with predictive modeling enables the creation of dynamic, individualized marketing strategies. Segmented groups identified by behavior analysis or clustering can be used to personalize offers, reactivation campaigns, or retention incentives (such as loyalty programs for at-risk customers). Predictive models output churn probabilities or likely future purchase classes, allowing e-commerce platforms to trigger timely interventions. Predictive insights inform pricing strategies (e.g., demand forecasting), product recommendations, and ad personalization, all aimed at improving conversion and lifetime customer value.

**In Summary**  
Machine learning in e-commerce customer segmentation and purchasing prediction succeeds by carefully selecting relevant customer features, designing models that combine robustness (often ensembles/hybrids), and addressing data sparsity through feature selection, oversampling, incremental learning, or fusion. These approaches generate actionable insights that underpin targeted, efficient, and profitability-driven marketing campaigns tailored to each customer's likely behavior.

1. Segment customers into actionable groups

2. Predict what customers are likely to do next

After segmentation, supervised models can estimate outcomes relevant to marketing, including purchase or repurchase probability, churn risk, customer lifetime value, conversion, preferences, demand, and product-return risk.

The evidence does not point to one universally best algorithm. Instead, it suggests matching the model to the structure of the problem:

Logistic regression provides a relatively simple approach to repurchase and purchase prediction.

CNN-BiLSTM and other deep-learning architectures can capture complex patterns and sequential dependencies in customer behavior.
Time-aware models incorporating seasonal indicators can better represent changing purchasing patterns during variable periods.

The resulting probabilities or risk scores provide a basis for deciding which customers to target and what type of intervention may be appropriate, rather than treating every customer identically.

3. Customer features are central to useful predictions

Transaction/value: recency, frequency, monetary value, total orders and spending.
Engagement: website time, sessions, app opens, browsing depth and click/navigation behavior.

Experience and retention signals: complaints, satisfaction, cashback, return rate and days since last purchase.
Product and commercial context: product preferences, price, discounts and product characteristics.
Temporal/contextual information: seasonal indicators and time-based behavioral measures.
Unstructured information: reviews and sentiment.

Effective design involves more than selecting an algorithm. The supplied studies highlight data cleaning, missing-value handling, encoding, normalization, feature selection, class balancing, sampling, cross-validation and appropriate performance metrics.

Class imbalance is particularly relevant when the outcome of interest, such as churn or purchase, is uncommon. Approaches described in the claims include balanced positive/negative samples, SMOTE, sampling techniques and probability-based model fusion. Model design also involves controlling overfitting. Hybrid and ensemble approaches are reported to improve robustness or generalization in several of the supplied studies.

Importantly, the appropriate optimization criterion can depend on the marketing objective. For example, one churn study emphasizes high precision to avoid spending retention resources on customers who are actually low risk, while other work emphasizes balancing precision and recall to identify customers who might otherwise be missed.

5. Data sparsity creates an important limit to personalization

The claims identify a critical qualification: finer customer segmentation improves predictive performance particularly for high-frequency users, but sparse data restrict the same gains for low-frequency users. One-to-one personalization therefore works best when enough observations exist to characterize an individual's behavior.

The supplied evidence describes hybrid recommendation architectures combining collaborative filtering, content-based information, sentiment/review analysis, matrix factorization and neural methods as ways of addressing data sparsity and cold-start problems.

Overall

Customer segmentation identifies meaningful behavioral groups; predictive models estimate purchase, repurchase, churn, value, or other future outcomes; feature analysis explains which customer characteristics are driving those predictions; and those outputs can guide personalized offers, recommendations, retention campaigns and allocation of marketing resources.

The main constraint is the interaction among these components: rich and well-engineered customer features provide the signal, appropriate model design extracts that signal while controlling imbalance and overfitting, and sufficient behavioral data determine how finely customers can be segmented and personalized. Consequently, effective targeted marketing depends not simply on using a more sophisticated algorithm, but on aligning segmentation granularity, feature quality, predictive modeling, interpretability, and the amount of customer data available.

anchor_claims.text: An image quality assessment (IQA)-guided single image super-resolution (SISR) method using deep learning networks achieves a balance between perceptual quality and distortion measures by integrating an IQA network to guide the adjustment of super-resolution network parameters.

The proposed method introduces an interactive training mechanism via a cascaded network, where the IQA network acts as a supervisor in constructing the loss function of the super-resolution network, addressing the issue of heterogeneous datasets used by IQA and SR networks.

A pairwise ranking hinge loss method is proposed to dynamically create training labels, overcoming the challenge of insufficient training samples and preventing overfitting during the training process.
The proposed method demonstrates a better tradeoff between perceptual quality and distortion measures compared to recent SISR methods, as evidenced by extensive benchmark experiments and analyses.

The architecture of the proposed method is flexible and not confined to a specific network model, allowing the baseline of the super-resolution network to be adjusted according to practical requirements, such as improving performance or enhancing efficiency.

## Summary: Single Image Super-Resolution Image Quality Assessment Deep Learning Network

The field of single image super-resolution (SISR) has increasingly integrated deep learning techniques to reconstruct high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs while balancing restored perceptual quality and objective metrics. A central advancement in this area is the use of **Image Quality Assessment (IQA) guided deep learning networks**, which incorporate dedicated IQA models to optimize, supervise, or evaluate the super-resolution (SR) process.

### Key Innovations and Approaches

- **IQA-Guided Training and Control**:  
  In the seminal paper "Single image super-resolution via Image Quality Assessment-Guided Deep Learning Network," an IQA network is integrated as a supervisor or loss component within the SR architecture. This guidance enables dynamic control over the SR model's parameters—such as loss weighting or optimization direction—based on current or target quality, thereby balancing perceptual similarity to high-quality references with suppression of artifacts. The framework addresses the challenge of training SR and IQA networks on heterogeneous datasets by dynamically aligning their objectives.

- **Interactive and Cascaded Architectures**:  
  Many variants adopt **cascaded or interactive architectures** where the IQA network assesses the intermediate or final SR output and adjusts subsequent processing stages. Some models use a pairwise ranking hinge loss that creates dynamically labeled targets to overcome the scarcity of training data and mitigate overfitting during super-resolution training.

- **Multi-Metric Optimization**:  
  Traditional SR models focus on objective metrics like PSNR and SSIM; however, recent deep learning-based methods also emphasize **perceptual assessments** (e.g., LPIPS or VDM) and incorporate **no-reference or proxy IQA losses** to better align with human visual judgment, especially in tasks like super-resolved medical or remote sensing images where ground truth is scarce.

- **Frequency and Feature-Based Assessment**:  
  Some approaches utilize frequency-domain features (high/low-frequency maps derived via Sobel or other operators) to construct IQA networks that explicitly learn what constitutes "high-quality" restoration at different scales. These frequency-aware IQA models help in guiding both single-stage and multi-stage SR networks and are often combined with Transformer or attention-based modules for global context modeling.

- **Model Flexibility and Efficiency**:  
  Proposed networks are often flexible in architecture, allowing for adaptations to different SR baselines (CNNs, transformers, hybrid models). The removal or modification of elements like batch normalization in SR generators can increase efficiency and generalization, sometimes reducing parameter count while retaining or improving perceptual quality.

### Benchmarking and Performance

- The IQA-guided SR models generally **achieve better trade-offs between objective and perceptual quality** compared to unguided or baselines like bicubic interpolation or simple GAN-based SR methods (e.g., SRGAN). They show **improved PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS scores**, alongside visually sharper and more natural reconstructions.
- Cross-dataset validation (e.g., CVIU, QADS, SRIJ) and generalization studies highlight the robustness of IQA-guided frameworks.
- Some methods introduce novel metrics such as the **Image Quality Difference (IDP)** specifically suited for comparing super-resolved MRI or other modalities where traditional metrics fail to capture perceptual differences.

### Challenges and Future Directions

- **Training Complexity**: Integrating IQA components can complicate training due to the heterogeneity of IQA and SR datasets and loss objectives.
- **Overfitting and Data Scarcity**: Solutions such as dynamic labeling via ranking hinge losses and knowledge distillation (e.g., from pre-trained models) help overcome limited labeled data for training both modules.
- **Real-World Applications**: Methods developed for medical (MRI, microscopy) and remote sensing imagery are often evaluated for both quantitative metrics and domain-specific perceptual tasks, underscoring the importance of robust IQA.

### Conclusion

**A deep learning network for single image super-resolution that incorporates image quality assessment components** offers a powerful means of balancing restoration fidelity and perceptual quality. By leveraging IQA for guidance, supervision, or evaluation, these networks achieve state-of-the-art results in both technical (PSNR, SSIM) and perceptual metrics, demonstrating substantial improvements over older and simpler methods. However, ongoing challenges remain in handling diverse and limited datasets, training stability, and real-time deployment.

This body of work underscores the synergy between image quality assessment and super-resolution deep learning and paves the way for more intelligent, adaptive, and robust image restoration pipelines.

---

Summary: Deep Learning-Based SISR and Image Quality Assessment

Single-image super-resolution (SISR) aims to reconstruct a high-resolution (HR) image from a single low-resolution (LR) observation. Because this reconstruction is inherently ill-posed, multiple plausible HR images can correspond to the same LR input. Deep learning has substantially improved SISR by learning nonlinear LR-to-HR mappings and progressively incorporating residual learning, dense connections, attention, Transformers, adversarial learning, and multi-scale feature extraction.

Early CNN-based approaches such as SRCNN demonstrated that feature extraction, nonlinear mapping, and image reconstruction could be jointly optimized in an end-to-end network. Subsequent residual architectures, particularly EDSR, improved reconstruction accuracy by removing unnecessary batch-normalization layers, introducing residual scaling, and adopting effective loss functions such as L1 loss. Dense and attention-based networks further strengthened the extraction of high-frequency information, while CNN-Transformer hybrid architectures combined CNNs' ability to recover local texture with Transformers' capacity to model long-range dependencies. Lightweight approaches additionally employ grouped convolution, re-parameterization, knowledge distillation, recursive structures, and efficient attention to reduce computational requirements.

A central challenge is that maximizing conventional distortion measures such as PSNR and SSIM does not necessarily produce images with the best perceptual quality. GAN-based and perceptual-loss approaches can generate sharper, visually appealing textures but sometimes obtain lower pixel-wise scores or introduce artificial details. Consequently, modern SISR research increasingly considers a perception-distortion tradeoff, using PSNR and SSIM together with perceptually oriented measures such as LPIPS and no-reference image quality indicators.

An important development is the direct integration of Image Quality Assessment (IQA) into the SISR learning process. In an IQA-guided cascaded framework, an IQA network is not merely used after reconstruction to evaluate the output. Instead, it operates as a supervisor for the SR network, contributing to the construction of its training objective and guiding parameter optimization toward perceptually preferable reconstructions. This interactive mechanism helps reconcile the heterogeneous datasets normally used to train SR and IQA models. Pairwise ranking with a hinge-based loss can dynamically construct supervisory labels, addressing limited IQA training samples and helping reduce overfitting. Because the IQA component can guide different SR backbones, this framework is also adaptable to networks selected either for maximum reconstruction quality or computational efficiency.

IQA itself has evolved toward deep, task-specific assessment of super-resolved imagery. Rather than relying exclusively on reference images, no-reference approaches can learn quality representations directly from reconstructed images. For example, frequency-aware assessment separates an SR image into high- and low-frequency maps, allowing a two-stream deep network to independently analyze fine details, edges and structural information. Features from complementary network levels can then be fused and regressed into an overall quality prediction. Cross-database evaluations indicate that such approaches can generalize beyond individual SR quality datasets.

Other learning-based IQA architectures exploit relationships between LR and SR images. The DISQ framework, for example, uses a two-stream network to extract information from both resolutions and combines the representations to predict perceived image quality. Large-scale dedicated SR quality databases such as SISAR further enable learning quality models that correlate more closely with subjective human judgments. These approaches demonstrate that quality assessment tailored specifically to super-resolution artifacts can provide information that conventional generic metrics may miss.

The literature also demonstrates that effective SISR depends on several complementary design principles:

Residual and dense learning improve gradient propagation and retention of hierarchical features.
Attention mechanisms emphasize informative channels, spatial regions, edges, and high-frequency structures.
CNN-Transformer hybrids jointly capture local image characteristics and global dependencies.
Multi-scale processing supports reconstruction across different spatial structures and magnification factors.
Perceptual, adversarial, edge, L1, Charbonnier, and IQA-guided losses offer alternatives to optimizing pixel-wise error alone.
No-reference and learned IQA provide more realistic assessments when ground-truth HR images are unavailable.
Efficient architectures, including grouped convolution, parameter sharing, re-parameterization, and distillation, improve suitability for real-time or edge deployment.
Domain-specific SR extends these concepts to remote sensing, MRI, infrared imaging, holographic microscopy, and artistic imagery.
Overall Research Trend

The literature collectively indicates a transition from “reconstruct first, assess afterward” toward quality-aware reconstruction, where image quality assessment becomes part of the learning loop:

Low-resolution image → SR deep network → reconstructed image → learned IQA network → perceptual-quality feedback → SR parameter optimization

This integration is particularly important because high numerical fidelity and high perceptual quality are not always equivalent. An IQA-guided deep SISR network can therefore optimize reconstruction according to both distortion and perceptual objectives rather than treating PSNR or SSIM as the sole measures of success.

Overall, the research suggests that the next generation of SISR systems should combine powerful reconstruction architectures with learned, perceptually meaningful quality assessment. Flexible IQA-guided optimization, robust no-reference assessment, efficient architectures, and quality metrics aligned with human perception provide a promising route toward SR models that recover fine structural detail while maintaining natural appearance, generalization, and practical computational efficiency.

Summary: Single-Image Super-Resolution, Image Quality Assessment, and Deep Learning Networks

Deep learning-based single-image super-resolution (SISR) reconstructs a high-resolution image from a single low-resolution input. Modern approaches have progressed from convolutional architectures such as SRCNN to residual, attention-based, GAN, and Transformer-based networks. These models improve feature extraction, recover high-frequency details, and model increasingly complex local and global image dependencies. However, because SISR is inherently ill-posed, optimizing conventional distortion measures such as PSNR and SSIM does not necessarily produce images with the best perceived visual quality. This has made image quality assessment (IQA) an important component of SISR research.

A key research direction is integrating learned IQA directly with super-resolution training. Rather than treating quality assessment solely as a post-processing evaluation step, an IQA network can provide perceptual supervision to the SR network, helping optimize reconstructed images toward a better balance between pixel-level fidelity and perceptual quality. Related research also uses no-reference or learned quality models that extract quality-sensitive information from features such as high- and low-frequency image components. Such approaches can complement traditional metrics and better characterize artifacts, sharpness, textures, and structural fidelity.

Across the broader literature, several architectural strategies support improved SISR quality:

Residual and dense connections facilitate training of deep networks and preserve hierarchical image information.
Attention mechanisms selectively emphasize informative spatial regions and feature channels.
CNN-Transformer hybrids combine CNN-based recovery of local textures with Transformer-based modeling of long-range dependencies.
Perceptual, edge, adversarial, and reconstruction losses allow networks to optimize different aspects of visual fidelity.
Lightweight and multi-scale architectures seek to retain reconstruction quality while reducing parameters and inference cost.
Quality-aware training and learned IQA provide alternatives to relying exclusively on PSNR or SSIM when perceptual realism is important.

Overall, the literature suggests that SISR is increasingly moving from maximizing a single distortion metric toward joint optimization of reconstruction accuracy, perceptual quality, and computational efficiency. Learned IQA provides a particularly promising mechanism for supplying quality-aware feedback during training and for evaluating super-resolved images when no perfect reference is available.

Important retraction caveat

The supplied metadata identifies “Single image super-resolution via Image Quality Assessment-Guided Deep Learning Network” as retracted. Therefore, its specific claims about an IQA-supervised cascaded training architecture, pairwise-ranking hinge loss, improved perceptual-distortion tradeoff, and architectural flexibility should not be treated as reliable evidence or used to support scientific conclusions without independent validation. These ideas may be discussed as claims made by the retracted work, but conclusions about SISR and IQA should instead be grounded in the non-retracted literature supplied in the context.

Bottom line

Deep-learning SISR seeks not merely to enlarge an image, but to reconstruct plausible high-frequency information while retaining fidelity to the source. Integrating perceptually meaningful image-quality assessment with modern residual, attention, and Transformer architectures offers a route toward models whose outputs score well quantitatively and look convincing perceptually, although evidence originating from the identified retracted paper must be excluded or explicitly qualified.

Rather than handling trade, financing, payments, inventory, and compliance as isolated activities, emerging network models connect exporters, importers, banks, logistics providers, regulators, suppliers, and digital marketplaces through shared information and analytical infrastructure.

A central feature of this transformation is the application of big data, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. Improved online k-means and related techniques address uncertainty and fuzziness in cross-border e-commerce data. Such forecasting can help firms optimize inventory, marketing, financial planning, and supply-chain decisions. Neural-network research further indicates that variables such as exchange rates, transportation capacity, and technological development can be incorporated into models for predicting or explaining international trade performance.

Digital trade platforms and e-commerce networks provide the operational foundation for these capabilities. Large marketplaces can reduce search, coordination, logistics, and transaction costs by exploiting network effects and economies of scale. International trade information-management systems similarly connect functions such as export operations, supplier management, inventory, transportation, documentation, customer management, and managerial decision-making. However, platform concentration can create risks involving market power, self-preferencing, data exploitation, privacy, digital taxation, counterfeiting, and unequal value distribution, making appropriate governance and international regulatory coordination important.

Within trade finance, technologies such as AI and blockchain can further digitalize payments and documentary processes. AI-based systems can support credit assessment, fraud detection, compliance monitoring, document processing, and predictive risk analysis. Blockchain and smart contracts offer a complementary architecture for sharing transaction information, maintaining auditable records, automating verification, and reducing dependence on paper-based processes such as traditional letters of credit. Collectively, these technologies have the potential to reduce processing delays, information asymmetry, operational costs, and human error.

A network perspective is also particularly valuable for risk and compliance. Trade-based money-laundering analysis can combine trade discrepancies, transaction clustering, network relationships, repeated counterparties, jurisdictions, and sector-specific indicators to identify suspicious patterns that may be difficult to discover through individual transaction screening. Strong institutional governance, regulatory controls, data protection, authentication, encryption, and transparent analytical systems are therefore important complements to technological innovation.

At a broader economic level, international trade cannot be understood solely as a sequence of bilateral transactions. Trade-network relationships can transmit and amplify economic and financial shocks, including international monetary-policy spillovers. Digital platforms deepen these interdependencies through data flows, algorithmic coordination, technical standards, supply-chain relationships, and global value chains. Consequently, network-enabled trade-finance systems can serve not only as transaction-processing platforms but also as infrastructures for monitoring interconnected financial, operational, and macroeconomic risks.

The greatest value comes from integrating commercial transactions with finance, logistics, forecasting, and compliance within the same digital ecosystem. At the same time, realizing these benefits requires strong cybersecurity, interoperable systems, transparent algorithms, data governance, regulatory coordination, and safeguards against platform concentration and systemic risk.

Three heuristic algorithms, NSGA-II-EDSP, NSGA-II-KES, and NSGA-II-QKES, are designed to improve the NSGA-II algorithm for solving multi-objective parallel flow shop scheduling problems, incorporating rules like shortest processing time and earliest due date, clustering techniques, and reinforcement learning for crossover rate optimization.

The proposed algorithms demonstrate improved performance in generating Pareto front solutions for multi-objective scheduling problems compared to the standard NSGA-II algorithm, with enhancements in solution quality, diversity, and computational efficiency.

The multi-objective scheduling optimization model incorporates employee workload balance as a critical factor, addressing psychological impacts and improving production efficiency and employee satisfaction.
The NSGA-II-QKES algorithm achieves the best optimization results among the proposed methods, with significant improvements in error ratio, solution span, and the number of non-dominated solutions.

**Summary: Multi-Objective Optimal Scheduling for Labor Workload Distribution Balance**

Research in multi-objective optimal scheduling increasingly emphasizes the importance of balancing labor workload distributions to improve workplace fairness, employee satisfaction, and operational efficiency. This approach addresses the complex trade-offs encountered in scheduling tasks or jobs across parallel flow shops, cloud environments, or distributed systems (e.g., radiology technicians, cloud computing, microgrids, and robotic disassembly lines), by simultaneously optimizing multiple objectives.

**Key Objectives and Models:**
- The primary objectives typically include minimizing total delay or makespan, as well as reducing the standard deviation of employee workloads. This serves to equitize labor distribution and mitigate overloading or under-utilization of workers.
- Multi-objective integer programming (MOIP) and advanced evolutionary metaheuristics—such as NSGA-II variants with enhanced operators (EDSP, KES, QKES), Hybrid Memetic Algorithms, Horse Herd Optimization (HOA), and bio-inspired algorithms (e.g., Squirrel Search, Migrating Birds Optimization)—are frequently developed and applied to model and solve these problems.
- These algorithms improve upon the classical NSGA-II by introducing strategies such as rule-based initial population sorting (e.g., shortest processing time, earliest due date), clustering and fuzzy logic for better exploration, reinforcement learning to adaptively tune parameters (e.g., crossover rates), and elite selection to maintain diversity while converging to the Pareto front.

**Benefits of Workload Balance:**
- Balancing labor workloads reduces workload inequality among employees, aligning with fairness and psychological well-being principles.
- It enhances overall productivity and job satisfaction by reducing fatigue, burnout, and monotony.
- Workload balance supports compliance with legal and institutional policies on fair labor practice and workforce equity.
- It helps address operational risks such as bottlenecks, over-exertion, or under-utilization that arise from unbalanced task assignment.

**Additional Enhancements in Contemporary Approaches:**
- Integration of physical and cognitive workload models (using metrics such as RULA for physical, task stiffness for cognitive) for more holistic balancing.
- Use of predictive models, reinforcement learning, and adaptive scheduling frameworks in cloud and distributed environments to dynamically respond to fluctuating workloads and SLA requirements.
- Incorporation of energy efficiency, environmental sustainability (especially relevant in green cloud and energy systems), and compliance considerations (e.g., carbon trading, legal constraints) into multi-objective frameworks.

**Performance and Impact:**
- Novel heuristic and metaheuristic algorithms demonstrate significant improvements over traditional methods in terms of solution quality, diversity of the Pareto front, and computational efficiency.
- Metrics such as reduced standard deviation in workload, lower total delay, improved throughputs, and energy savings validate the effectiveness of workload-balanced scheduling.
- These methods also achieve better convergence and stability, making them suitable for both small and large-scale applications in healthcare, manufacturing, distributed energy, and cloud infrastructures.

**Conclusion:**
Multi-objective optimal scheduling frameworks that focus on balancing labor workload distribution have emerged as critical tools for modern operations management. By jointly optimizing efficiency and equity, these approaches not only enhance organizational performance but also foster healthier and more sustainable work environments. The integration of advanced optimization and heuristic techniques continues to expand the capabilities of such scheduling systems, addressing real-world complexities in workforce management across diverse domains.

**Summary: Multi-Objective Optimal Scheduling with Labor Workload Distribution Balance**

The research titled "Research on multi-objective optimal scheduling considering the balance of labor workload distribution" addresses the complex challenge of optimizing workforce scheduling in environments with multiple conflicting objectives. The study develops a **bi-objective nonlinear integer programming model** specifically aimed at optimizing parallel flow shop scheduling. Its primary goal is to **minimize both total delay time and the standard deviation of employee workload distributions**, thereby explicitly balancing efficiency (through reduced delays) and fairness/health (by leveling the distribution of workloads among employees).

To tackle the inherent trade-offs and computational complexity of this multi-objective setting, the authors propose three **heuristic algorithms**—NSGA-II-EDSP, NSGA-II-KES, and NSGA-II-QKES—that build upon the classic NSGA-II metaheuristic. These enhanced algorithms incorporate advanced techniques such as:

- **Rule-based improvements (e.g., Shortest Processing Time and Earliest Due Date rules)** to inform the initial population and scheduling process.

Multi-objective optimization therefore aims to identify Pareto-optimal schedules representing different compromises between efficiency and workload equity.
